subject.title: Writ on the Steps of Puerto Rican Harlem
subject.author: Gregory Corso
subject.text:
There's a truth limits man
A truth prevents his going any farther   
The world is changing
The world knows it's changing
Heavy is the sorrow of the day
The old have the look of doom
The young mistake their fate in that look   
That is truth
But it isn't all truth

Life has meaning
And I do not know the meaning   
Even when I felt it were meaningless
I hoped and prayed and sought a meaning
It wasn't all frolic poesy
There were dues to pay   
Summoning Death and God   
I'd a wild dare to tackle Them
Death proved meaningless without Life
Yes the world is changing   
But Death remains the same   
It takes man away from Life   
The only meaning he knows   
And usually it is a sad business   
This Death

I'd an innocence I'd a seriousness
I'd a humor save me from amateur philosophy
I am able to contradict my beliefs   
I am able able
Because I want to know the meaning of everything
Yet sit I like a brokenness   
Moaning: Oh what responsibility   
I put on thee Gregory
Death and God
Hard hard it's hard

I learned life were no dream
I learned truth deceived
Man is not God   
Life is a century   
Death an instant

title: Everything Here Is Abstract Except the Address
standfirst: Gregory Corso's poem argues with Death and God without describing a single street, face or building. The steps in its title were real, though — a stretch of East Harlem that had just finished changing from the largest Italian colony in America into Puerto Rican Harlem.

sections.heading: Steps That Had Already Changed Hands
sections.body:
Nothing in Gregory Corso's poem says where it happens. Death, God, a truth that limits man, the young mistaking their fate in the look of the old — the whole argument could be made from any city on Earth. Only the title fixes a location: the steps of Puerto Rican Harlem, a stretch of East Harlem that had spent the previous two decades changing hands.

Corso's poem appeared in *Long Live Man* in 1962, by which time those blocks had already been through one entire population. From the 1870s they were Italian Harlem, the country's largest Italian-American colony — [more than 110,000 people at its 1930s peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Harlem), eighty-one percent of them first- or second-generation immigrants, according to that year's census. Puerto Rican migration, under way since the First World War, filled the same streets as postwar tenement clearance pushed Italian families out to the Bronx, Brooklyn and New Jersey; by 1950 the Puerto Rican population had reached 63,000, and by the decade Corso was writing in, Spanish Harlem was already the name outsiders used for the whole district, not just its original western edge.

The poem gives none of that. No bodega, no market stall, no single Puerto Rican voice — just a title naming one very specific piece of pavement, attached to a meditation that never once looks down at it.

sections.heading: Eleven Years, Five Addresses, Then a Cell
sections.body:
Corso's own geography, across those same years, was unstable for entirely different reasons. He was born Nunzio Corso in 1930 at St. Vincent's Hospital, to two teenage parents who lived at the corner of Bleecker and MacDougal — [Greenwich Village's own Italian quarter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregory_Corso), a few miles downtown from the steps this poem is named for. His mother left within his first year; his father told him, at different times, that she had abandoned the family for Italy and, separately, that she had become a prostitute driven into exile. Neither was true, though Corso would not learn that for another sixty-seven years, when a filmmaker retracing Beat history located her alive in New Jersey.

In the meantime, his father put him into foster care, visited rarely, and once told him he should have flushed him down the toilet. Corso spent the next eleven years cycling through at least five foster homes, and by his own account was beaten on both sides of every visit: *I'd spill jello, and the foster home people would beat me. Then my father would visit, and he'd beat me again — a double whammy.* At eleven he moved back in with his remarried father; by his teens he had run away and was sleeping in the subway in winter and on rooftops in summer around Little Italy, still attending Catholic school without telling anyone where he slept. At seventeen, arrested for stealing a suit, he was sentenced to two to three years at Clinton State Prison in Dannemora — and it was there, in a cell recently vacated by Lucky Luciano, reading whatever Luciano's donated library and his own hunger put in front of him, that Corso became a poet.

sections.heading: Tackling Death and Getting a Draw
sections.body:
The poem stops being vague exactly once. *Summoning Death and God*, Corso writes, capitalizing both like parties to a court case, *I'd a wild dare to tackle Them.* What follows is not a victory. *Death proved meaningless without Life*, the poem decides — then immediately qualifies it: *But Death remains the same / It takes man away from Life... The only meaning he knows / And usually it is a sad business / This Death.* A capitalized cosmic antagonist, built up over several lines, lands on "a sad business" — about as flat a description as English allows.

That swing between grand stakes and flat understatement was Corso's habit two years before this poem reached print, too. New Directions published *The Happy Birthday of Death* in 1960 with [a jacket description](https://www.ndbooks.com/book/the-happy-birthday-of-death/) that reads, in hindsight, like a note on this poem specifically: like Villon or Dylan Thomas, it says, Corso lives close to the mystery of death, and it is perhaps his central theme, on which variations ranging from the terrible to the comic are sounded — but Corso is seldom macabre, because a bursting vitality always carries him back to the sensations of the living. "Writ on the Steps" runs that exact pattern in miniature: dare Death and God, flinch from the cosmic, land on the sensation of being alive and finding the whole exercise a sad business.

sections.heading: The Moment "Man" Becomes "Gregory"
sections.body:
For three stanzas the poem argues on behalf of "man" in general — *There's a truth limits man*, the opening line says, not *me*. That holds until the third stanza starts to buckle: *I am able to contradict my beliefs / I am able able* — the same four words twice, the second time with no verb to finish the thought. Corso once described his own approach to sound [this way](https://www.ndbooks.com/book/the-happy-birthday-of-death/): "It's not the metre or measure of a line, a breath; not 'law' music; but the assembly of great eye sounds placed into an inspired measured idea." Whatever that repetition is, it reads like speech catching on itself rather than a scansion decision.

Then the poem drops the universal claim altogether. *Yet sit I like a brokenness / Moaning: Oh what responsibility / I put on thee Gregory / Death and God.* "Man" disappears. In its place is Gregory — not Nunzio, the name his family in Little Italy used, but Gregory, the confirmation name he had chosen for himself. The poem's opening claim, that this is a truth about man in the abstract, holds for exactly as long as it takes Corso to run out of road and address himself, by name, for the debt he has just taken on.

sections.heading: Printed Inside a Book Called Long Live Man
sections.body:
"Writ on the Steps of Puerto Rican Harlem" appeared in *Long Live Man*, Corso's 1962 collection. New Directions [sold the book](https://www.ndbooks.com/book/long-live-man/) on a single defiant sentence: "Long live Man! sings the poet Gregory Corso – despite atom bombs and computers, cold wars that get hot and togetherness that isn't, too many cars and too little love… and in these poems he celebrates the wonders (and the laughs and griefs) of being a man alive." Allen Ginsberg's blurb for the same book called Corso "an aphoristic poet, and a poet of ideas," and asked what other modern poets wrote "with such terse clarity that their verses stick in the mind without effort."

The poem's own ending is the proof of Ginsberg's claim, whatever the publisher meant by it: *I learned life were no dream / I learned truth deceived / Man is not God / Life is a century / Death an instant.* Five lines, three flat aphorisms, no hedging — and, set against a cover line promising that man lives long, a strange note to end on. Not a defiant long live man so much as an exact description of how short the living turns out to be, and how long it can take to find out what was actually true. Corso, whose own father's lies about his mother held for sixty-seven years, had reason to know.
